title: Cube Counter
context: Grade 5, the first volume page and Exercise 8.4's counted blocks. An adult sees counting. What the page is doing is naming a third measure: the volume is the space a solid takes up, counted in unit cubes, and every cube counts whether it can be seen or not.

writeup.why: Meet volume as the space a solid takes up, pick the unit cube that fits, find a volume by counting unit cubes by rows, and count the cubes hidden in a stack.
writeup.look: Solids drawn in three faces with a tray of violet unit cubes under them, a unit shelf on the second phase, and the Lift layer control and See-through switch on the last two.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Cube Counter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of cubes counted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The solids stand on a table top drawn along y 640, in three visible faces at x 160, y 260 inside a box 600 by 380, every unit cube 44 across. The tray of violet unit cubes, each labelled Unit cube, runs along y 680 from x 120. On the first phase the two open boxes stand at x 160 and x 480 with a counter under each, and the Fill button at x 820, y 250. On the second phase the unit shelf stands at x 820, y 330 with three cubes labelled by their edges, beside a picture card at x 160, y 260. On the later phases a tapped row lights amber as it is counted; the Lift layer control at x 820, y 420 lifts the top layer up and to the right, lit amber and labelled Layer; and the See-through switch at x 820, y 500 draws every cube in outline. The volume reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with cu. mm, cu. cm and cu. m keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last solid stands rebuilt with every cube counted, and the volume in green with its cubic unit.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the last layer is lifted, the lifted layers stand in a neat row and each one gives a small hop as its count is added.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet counted. On the first phase two open boxes stand side by side, empty, with the Fill button. On the second the unit shelf stands beside a picture card. On the third a solid of unit cubes stands on the table top, its rows uncounted. On the fourth a stack stands with only its front faces showing and the Lift layer control beside it. One thing moves, once: the Fill button, the unit shelf or the Lift layer control gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any solid built from the tray, filled, lifted apart or seen through. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on space taken up, units of volume, counting cubes by rows and counting hidden cubes.

serves.exercise: finding three volumes by counting unit cubes

source_tool.description: Solids are drawn in three visible faces on a warm white ground, every unit cube the same size. A tray of violet unit cubes, each labelled Unit cube, sits under the working area. On the first phase two open solids stand side by side and a Fill button pours cubes into the chosen one until it is full, with a counter under each. A unit shelf holds three cubes with edges of 1 mm, 1 cm and 1 m, drawn as labels rather than to scale, beside a picture card of the thing to be measured. On the later phases a solid is built from unit cubes; the child taps a row to count it, and a Lift layer control lifts the top layer up and aside, so the layer beneath comes into view, with the lifted layer lit amber and labelled Layer. A See-through switch draws every cube in outline so the hidden ones show. A number pad types a count or a volume with cu. mm, cu. cm and cu. m keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of cubes counted.
source_tool.art_direction: Wooden cubes on a classroom table / Picture book

The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lift the layers and look again. Did every cube get counted once?
voice.onNext: A new solid. Count it row by row.
voice.opening: Some solids, and a tray of unit cubes.
voice.onFinish: You measured space by the cubes that fill it, hidden ones too.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Build a stack and count every cube.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has filled a small box with unit cubes or sugar cubes and built a stack behind a card for a partner to guess. The tool is what lifts a stack apart layer by layer, so the hidden cubes are counted rather than guessed.

answer_key.rule: The volume of a solid is the amount of space it takes up. A cube whose edges are all 1 cm long is a unit cube, with a volume of 1 cu. cm; volume is measured in cubic units, cu. mm for very small things, cu. cm for small ones and cu. m for large ones. The number of unit cubes that fill a solid is its volume; count them by rows and layers. Cubes hidden behind or under others take up space and are counted too.
answer_key.wrong: The child's count stays, and the stage lifts the solid apart layer by layer beside it, lighting amber the row or layer that was missed or counted twice. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Fill both boxes with unit cubes of one size.
The shoebox holds far more cubes than the pencil box.
So the shoebox takes up more space, and the amount of space a solid takes up is its volume.
items.answer: The shoebox. The space a solid takes up is its volume
items.question: A shoebox and a pencil box sit side by side. Which takes up more space, and what is that space called?
items.checkpoint: Volume is the space a solid takes up.
items.misconception: Choosing the longer box, though a long thin box can take up less space than a short wide one.

steps: A unit cube with edges of 1 mm is tiny, about the size of a grain of sugar.
A unit cube with edges of 1 cm is about the size of a die.
A unit cube with edges of 1 m is large, so a classroom is measured in cu. m.
items.question: Which unit fits the volume of a classroom: cu. mm, cu. cm or cu. m?
items.checkpoint: Very small things use cu. mm, small ones cu. cm and large ones cu. m.
items.misconception: Choosing cu. cm because it is the unit met most often, though a classroom would need far too many of them to count.

steps: Count the cubes that fill it, row by row.
Each is 1 cu. cm, so the volume is 18 cu. cm.
items.question: A solid is built from unit cubes of 1 cm: 9 in a row, and 2 such rows side by side, one cube high. What is its volume?
items.checkpoint: Count every cube that fills the solid.
items.misconception: Counting the faces that can be seen instead of the cubes, which counts some cubes more than once.

steps: Take the stack apart layer by layer.
Each layer has 6 cubes, seen or hidden.
4 x 6 = 24, so 24 unit cubes fill it.
So its volume is 24 cu. cm, counting the hidden ones.
items.question: A stack has 4 layers with 6 cubes of 1 cm in each layer. Some cubes are hidden. What is its volume?
items.checkpoint: Hidden cubes take up space too.
items.misconception: Counting only the cubes that can be seen from the front, which leaves the hidden ones out.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which takes up more space: a school bag or a pencil?
items.final_answer: The school bag. It has the greater volume

items.question: What is the volume of a unit cube whose edges are 1 m long?
A row of 7 unit cubes of 1 cm lies on a desk. What is its volume?
Which unit fits the volume of a grain of sugar: cu. mm, cu. cm or cu. m?
A solid is built from 2 rows of 10 unit cubes of 1 cm, side by side. What is its volume?
A stack has 3 layers with 9 cubes in each layer. How many unit cubes fill it?
A stack is 2 layers high with 11 cubes in each layer, and some are hidden. How many unit cubes fill it?
items.final_answer: 2 x 11 = 22, so 22 unit cubes, hidden ones included

items.question: A solid is built from 4 rows of 9 unit cubes of 1 cm, side by side. What is its volume?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: pours unit cubes into the chosen solid until it is full
picks a unit cube with edges of 1 mm, 1 cm or 1 m for a thing to be measured
counts one row of cubes and adds it to the running count
lifts the top layer up and aside to show the layer beneath
draws every cube in outline so hidden cubes show
types a count or a volume, with cu. mm, cu. cm and cu. m keys

teaching_notes: Fill a small box with unit cubes before the tool opens; the count is the volume. Say the unit every time, cu. cm for a small box and cu. m for a room. Count by rows and layers, never by the faces that can be seen, and build a stack, then take it apart layer by layer, to check the hidden cubes. Keep the three measures apart: a length, a surface and a space. The printed blocks are the child's to count.
